questions.q: According to this lesson, what actually changes about PAM mechanisms like vaulting and JIT activation when moving from one team to enterprise scale?
options: The underlying mechanisms stay the same; what changes is the surface they have to cover, across many business units and systems
Vaulting and JIT activation stop working and have to be replaced with different mechanisms entirely
Session recording becomes unnecessary once an organization grows past one team
Access reviews are only needed for small organizations, not enterprise ones
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that vaulting, JIT activation, and access reviews don't change in principle at scale — what changes is the much larger and more varied surface those same mechanisms now have to be applied across.

questions.q: Why does an enterprise need a role catalog, according to this lesson?
options: A role catalog is required by law in every jurisdiction
It eliminates the need for session recording
Without a consistent, central inventory of what each privileged role grants, teams build incompatible roles that make basic questions about access unanswerable
It replaces the need for a PAM vault entirely
questions.explain: A role catalog gives every privileged role a consistent definition across the enterprise, which is what makes centralized JIT policy and access reviews possible in the first place.

questions.q: What is a segregation-of-duties (SoD) conflict, as described in this lesson?
options: A technical error in how a firewall rule is written
One person holding two roles that should never be combined, such as creating a vendor and approving payments to that vendor
A disagreement between two approvers over a single JIT request
A failure to rotate a privileged account's password on schedule
questions.explain: SoD conflicts arise when a single person holds two roles that, combined, enable fraud or error that neither role alone would allow — a risk only visible across the whole role catalog, not one request at a time.

questions.q: Why are break-glass accounts deliberately excluded from an organization's normal JIT approval flow?
options: Because break-glass accounts are reserved for the lowest-risk, routine administrative tasks
Because they are only used by external vendors, never internal staff
Because the normal approval chain doesn't need any oversight at all
Because they exist for emergencies where the approval system or identity provider itself may be unavailable, so they must be able to bypass that system
questions.explain: Break-glass accounts exist specifically for the scenario where the normal approval infrastructure is down, so by design they can't depend on that same infrastructure to grant access.

questions.q: What does the lesson say replaces the normal approval-chain accountability for a break-glass account, since that account skips the approval chain itself?
options: Nothing — break-glass accounts are intentionally left unmonitored
A separate vault, immediate credential rotation after use, and a mandatory alert and after-action review every time the account is used
A quarterly access review is the only control applied to break-glass accounts
Break-glass accounts are deleted automatically after a single use
questions.explain: Because break-glass access skips the normal request/approval flow, accountability is instead built around the account itself: separate vaulting, immediate rotation after use, and a mandatory alert plus after-action review on every use.
